Listen to this article Share Ugo Udezue’s election as Vice President of the Nigeria Basketball Federation (NBBF) places one of the game’s most widely travelled insiders at the heart of a new administration: a former international, ex-NBA agent and sports entrepreneur who has spent more than two decades on almost every side of the sport. Udezue was returned unopposed as vice president at the federation’s elective congress in Abuja on Thursday, 15 October 2026, as the sole candidate for the position. Earlier in the process, he was re-elected as the South-East zonal representative on the NBBF Board. He will serve alongside Dr Mustapha Abdullahi, Director-General of the Energy Commission of Nigeria, who won the presidency to succeed Engr. Ahmadu Musa Kida after eight years in office. Where Abdullahi brings experience in public administration and policy, Udezue brings the view from the court, the agent’s table and the boardroom. Together, the pairing gives the federation a blend of institutional management and commercial knowledge at a time when Nigerian basketball faces pressing demands for stronger leagues, better player welfare and reliable funding. Their shared goal is ambitious: a basketball ecosystem in which a Nigerian player can build a good living at home, without having to travel overseas to make a career of the game. The challenge before Udezue is to turn that ambition into structures that outlast any single administration. From the hardwood to the NBA Udezue’s journey began as a player. A product of Nigeria’s youth programme, he represented Nigeria at Under-18 level, an experience he has often said changed his life, before going on to play for the senior national team. He moved to the United States and went on to star for the University of Wyoming, where he studied public relations with a focus on advertising and communications. A 6 ft 8 in forward, he became one of the leading scorers in American college basketball, earning second-team All-WAC honours and averaging over 20 points a game. He later played professionally before injury brought his playing days to a close. His next chapter took him to the business side of the NBA. Bill Duffy, founder of BDA Sports Management, one of the most respected basketball agencies in the world, hired him in 2003. Udezue became the first Nigerian certified as an NBA agent in the United States and rose to vice president at BDA, representing athletes for more than 17 years. His client list included NBA players such as Nenê, Andre Roberson and Nigerian-born centre Festus Ezeli. That career gave him a working knowledge of contracts, sponsorship, player development and the commercial engine that powers professional basketball, knowledge he would later bring home. Building a league and a brand In 2017, Udezue stepped away from the comfort of the American game to pursue a bigger idea: a professional league for Africa. He co-founded the African Basketball League with six teams, later rebranding it as the Continental Basketball League (CBL), which grew to ten teams across six African countries. Before the league, he noted that Nigerians did not pay to watch basketball games. The league also gave birth to an unplanned business. Unable to secure shoe, apparel or even ball sponsors for the competition, Udezue and his partners created their own. AFA Sports, short for “Africa for Africa”, began by making uniforms and shoes for the league and soon became a kit partner to Nigeria’s national teams. Under his leadership as CEO, AFA Sports has manufactured in Lagos rather than outsourcing production, kitted the D’Tigers and D’Tigress, including the women’s team at the Tokyo Olympics, and signed an apparel partnership with the Ghana Basketball Association, extending its reach across the continent. Udezue’s argument has been consistent: African sport needs indigenous brands invested in its growth, rather than waiting on global giants to come to the rescue. A seat at the federation’s table Udezue’s involvement in federation affairs has deepened steadily. He was first elected South-East representative on the NBBF Board in 2022 and has served, pro bono, as Chairman of the federation’s Sponsorship and Marketing Committee, leading its drive for corporate partnerships. In March 2026, the Ebonyi State Sports Council appointed him Board Chairman of the Ebonyi State Basketball Association. His candidacy for vice president also carried regional significance: he positioned himself as a voice for the South-East, a region that produces a large share of Nigeria’s basketball talent. Ahead of the congress, Udezue publicly endorsed Abdullahi for the presidency, arguing that the sport needed stronger commercial structures, infrastructure and professional management. Nigeria, he pointed out, has more than 220 million people, with half of them under nineteen; a demographic he regards as the game’s greatest untapped asset. Keeping talent at home For Udezue, the work with Abdullahi is about more than running the NBBF. It is about building an industry. For decades, Nigeria’s best players have had to leave the country to earn a living from the game, playing in American colleges, European leagues and beyond, while the domestic game struggled to pay salaries, fill arenas or hold on to its stars. “Our dream is an ecosystem where a basketball player in Nigeria can live a very good life in Nigeria without travelling overseas,” Udezue said. “To do that, we have to develop our infrastructure and keep our talent in-house.” He sees infrastructure as the foundation of that ecosystem. Modern arenas create match-day revenue and television products. Professional clubs create salaried jobs for players, coaches, referees and staff. A credible league gives sponsors and investors a reason to commit. Each piece, he argues, makes the next one possible, and together they give young Nigerians a reason to build their careers at home. The commercial agenda Udezue’s stated ambition is to move the NBBF from a bureaucracy to a commercial enterprise, with the Board setting policy and full-time professional staff executing it. Central to that vision is the domestic Premier League. He has proposed transitioning it from a Board-run competition into an equity-driven company capable of attracting sponsors and investors. He also wants the national teams, the D’Tigers and the D’Tigress, and the Under-18 and Under-16 sides, managed as a sports business, with dedicated leadership, multi-year planning, and professional departments for logistics, scouting and administration. His platform also includes basketball infrastructure across the six geopolitical zones through partnerships with state governments and private capital, a national digital database of players, coaches, referees and clubs, and digital platforms for competitions, statistics and streaming. He has called for former internationals and members of the diaspora to play a greater role in scouting, technical matters and youth development, and for finance professionals and other high-profile figures to support the federation through advisory councils. He has pointed to the growth of the Basketball Africa League and rising investment in African basketball as evidence of the commercial opportunity available to Nigeria. The test ahead Few Nigerian administrators have seen the game from as many angles as Udezue: player, agent, league founder, kit manufacturer and federation official. That breadth gives him unusual credibility with players, investors and international partners alike. But the measure of his tenure will be practical. Professional staff must be hired and funded, the Premier League must become attractive to investors, and the national teams must be supported by systems rather than goodwill. Commercial growth will depend on the federation’s ability to demonstrate sound governance and deliver value to partners. For Udezue, the defining test will be whether he and Abdullahi can build an ecosystem in which Nigeria’s next generation of players no longer has to leave home to live well from the game.
